grammar_rules.rule_name: Formation of the present subjunctive for regular verbs
grammar_rules.summary: Add subjunctive endings (-e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent) to the stem from the 3rd person plural of the present indicative for je/tu/il/ils, and to the stem from the 1st person plural for nous/vous.
grammar_rules.explanation: The stem for je, tu, il/elle, ils/elles is found by dropping the -ent ending from the third-person plural present indicative form. The stem for nous and vous is found by dropping the -ons from the first-person plural of the present indicative. The present subjunctive for nous and vous is identical to the imparfait forms.
grammar_rules.formation: je/tu/il/ils: stem from ils/elles present indicative (drop -ent) + -e, -es, -e, -ent; nous/vous: stem from nous present indicative (drop -ons) + -ions, -iez
usage: Used to express subjective actions, wishes, emotions, doubt, etc.
exceptions: Irregular verbs have different stems or endings (see related rules).
common_traps: The nous/vous forms of present subjunctive are identical to the imparfait.

attestations.source_text: For most verbs, the present of the subjunctive is formed by adding the subjunctive endings (-e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent) to the stem. The stem for je, tu, il/elle, ils/elles is found by dropping the -ent ending from the third-person plural present indicative form. ... The stem for the nous and vous subjunctive forms is found by dropping the -ons from the first-person plural of the present indicative.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Irregular present subjunctive of être and avoir
grammar_rules.summary: Être and avoir have irregular stems and endings in the present subjunctive.
grammar_rules.explanation: The forms are: être: je sois, tu sois, il/elle soit, nous soyons, vous soyez, ils/elles soient; avoir: j'aie, tu aies, il/elle ait, nous ayons, vous ayez, ils/elles aient.
grammar_rules.formation: Irregular stems and endings; no regular pattern.
common_traps: Do not use indicative forms for subjunctive.

attestations.source_text: Être (to be) and avoir (to have) have both irregular stems and endings. [Table showing full conjugations]

grammar_rules.rule_name: Irregular present subjunctive of pouvoir, savoir, faire
grammar_rules.summary: These verbs have irregular stems but regular endings in the present subjunctive.
grammar_rules.explanation: pouvoir: je puisse, tu puisses, il/elle puisse, nous puissions, vous puissiez, ils/elles puissent; savoir: je sache, tu saches, il/elle sache, nous sachions, vous sachiez, ils/elles sachent; faire: je fasse, tu fasses, il/elle fasse, nous fassions, vous fassiez, ils/elles fassent.

attestations.source_text: The following three verbs have an irregular subjunctive stem but regular endings. [Tables for pouvoir, savoir, faire]

grammar_rules.rule_name: Irregular present subjunctive of aller and vouloir
grammar_rules.summary: Aller and vouloir have irregular stems in je/tu/il/ils forms and are partially irregular in nous/vous.
grammar_rules.explanation: aller: j'aille, tu ailles, il/elle aille, nous allions, vous alliez, ils/elles aillent; vouloir: je veuille, tu veuilles, il/elle veuille, nous voulions, vous vouliez, ils/elles veuillent.
grammar_rules.formation: Irregular stem in singular and third-person plural; nous/vous use a different stem.

attestations.source_text: Aller (to go) and vouloir (to want) have an irregular stem in the je, tu, il/elle, ils/elles forms and are partially irregular in the nous and vous forms. [Tables]

grammar_rules.rule_name: Use of subjunctive after verbs of wish and desire
grammar_rules.summary: The subjunctive is used after verbs expressing wish/desire when the subject of the main clause differs from that of the dependent clause.
grammar_rules.explanation: If the subject is the same, an infinitive is used instead. Examples: Je veux acheter... (same subject) vs Je veux que tu achètes... (different subject).
grammar_rules.formation: Main clause verb of wish + que + subjunctive clause (different subjects).
usage: Expressing wish, desire, demand, etc. with different subjects.
restrictions: Only when subjects are different; otherwise use infinitive.
conditions: Main clause subject ≠ dependent clause subject.
common_traps: Forgetting to use subjunctive when subjects differ.

attestations.section_title: Subjunctive after verbs of wish and desire
attestations.source_text: The subjunctive is used after verbs expressing the notion of wish and desire. It is used when the subject of the main clause is different from the subject of the dependent clause. Compare: Je veux acheter cet ordinateur. / Je veux que tu achètes cet ordinateur.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Use of subjunctive after expressions of emotion
grammar_rules.summary: The subjunctive is used after expressions of emotion.
grammar_rules.explanation: Expressions of emotion such as regretter, être ravi, être déçu, être content, etc. are followed by que + subjunctive.

attestations.source_text: The subjunctive is used after expressions of emotion.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Use of subjunctive after expressions of doubt
grammar_rules.summary: The subjunctive is used after expressions of doubt.
grammar_rules.explanation: Verbs like douter, ne pas croire, ne pas penser, etc. are followed by the subjunctive.

attestations.source_text: The subjunctive is also used after expressions of doubt.

grammar_rules.summary: Penser and croire in the affirmative are followed by the indicative; in negative or interrogative, the subjunctive may be used to express uncertainty.
grammar_rules.explanation: Affirmative: Je pense qu'il vient (indicative). Negative: Je ne pense pas qu'il vienne (subjunctive) may indicate doubt. The choice can convey different degrees of certainty.
grammar_rules.formation: Affirmative: penser/croire + que + indicative. Negative/interrogative: ne pas penser/croire + que + subjunctive (optional).
restrictions: Subjunctive in negative/interrogative is optional and indicates more uncertainty.
conditions: Negative or interrogative form of penser/croire.

attestations.source_text: The verbs penser (to think) and croire (to believe) in the affirmative are followed by the indicative mood. However, in the negative and interrogative, the subjunctive can be used to underline the uncertainty of the event. Je ne crois pas que Daniel est coupable. / Je ne crois pas que Daniel soit coupable.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Impersonal expressions followed by the indicative
grammar_rules.summary: Certain impersonal expressions are followed by the indicative mood.
grammar_rules.explanation: Expressions expressing certainty, probability, or evidence: il est certain, il est sûr, il est évident, il est vrai, il est probable, il me semble.

attestations.source_text: Here are some impersonal expressions that are followed by the indicative: il est certain, il est sûr, il est évident, il est vrai, il est probable, il me semble.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Impersonal expressions followed by the subjunctive
grammar_rules.summary: Certain impersonal expressions are followed by the subjunctive mood.
grammar_rules.explanation: Expressions expressing will, obligation, necessity, emotion, doubt: il faut, il est possible, il est essentiel, il est indispensable, il est juste, il se peut, il est important, il vaut mieux, il est préférable, il est souhaitable, il est naturel, il est normal, il est rare, il est utile, il est étrange, il est bizarre, il est étonnant, il est surprenant, il est triste, il est dommage, il est regrettable, cela ne vaut pas la peine.
signal_words: cela ne vaut pas la peine que
common_traps: Forgetting to use subjunctive after these expressions.

attestations.source_text: Here are some impersonal expressions that are followed by the subjunctive: il faut, il est possible, il est essentiel, il est indispensable, il est juste, il se peut, il est important, il vaut mieux, il est préférable, il est souhaitable, il est naturel, il est normal, il est rare, il est utile, il est étrange, il est bizarre, il est étonnant, il est surprenant, il est triste, il est dommage, il est regrettable, cela ne vaut pas la peine.

grammar_rules.summary: A list of conjunctions that require the subjunctive in the following clause.
grammar_rules.explanation: Conjunctions: afin que, pour que, de peur que, de crainte que, avant que, jusqu'à ce que, bien que, quoique, sans que, à moins que, pourvu que, à condition que, en attendant que.
usage: Expressing purpose, fear, time, concession, condition, etc.
common_traps: Confusing with conjunctions that take the indicative (see Chapter 9).

attestations.source_text: When you use conjunctions, you will also have to decide whether to use the indicative or the subjunctive in the following clause. [List of conjunctions]

grammar_rules.summary: Pourvu que is a conjunction meaning 'provided that' and is followed by the subjunctive.
grammar_rules.explanation: In a two-clause construction, pourvu que introduces a condition.
grammar_rules.formation: Main clause + pourvu que + subjunctive clause.

attestations.source_text: Pourvu que has the sense of provided that.

grammar_rules.summary: When used in a single clause, pourvu que expresses hope and is followed by the subjunctive.
grammar_rules.explanation: Pourvu que + subjunctive can be used as an exclamation to express a wish or hope.

attestations.source_text: When used in a single clause, pourvu que takes a different meaning. It is a handy expression, also followed by the subjunctive, that expresses hopes and desires.

grammar_rules.summary: The subjunctive is used after a superlative or an adjective conveying a superlative idea.
grammar_rules.explanation: Adjectives like premier, dernier, seul, unique, etc. trigger the subjunctive in the relative clause.
usage: Expressing a subjective evaluation or uniqueness.

attestations.section_title: Subjunctive after superlatives and in relative clauses
attestations.source_text: The subjunctive is also used after a superlative or an adjective conveying a superlative idea, such as: premier (first), dernier (last), seul (only), unique (unique), etc.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Subjunctive in relative clauses with doubt
grammar_rules.summary: The subjunctive may be used after relative pronouns when there is doubt about the existence or realization of the antecedent.
grammar_rules.explanation: If the existence of the person/thing is uncertain, use the subjunctive.

attestations.section_title: Subjunctive after superlatives and in relative clauses
attestations.source_text: The relative pronouns qui and que can sometimes be followed by the subjunctive. If there is some doubt about the existence of someone or the possible realization of something, the subjunctive may be used after the relative pronoun.

grammar_rules.summary: The past subjunctive is formed with the present subjunctive of avoir or être + past participle.
grammar_rules.explanation: Use the same auxiliary as in the passé composé. Agreement rules apply with être.
grammar_rules.formation: Present subjunctive of avoir/être + past participle.
usage: For actions anterior to the main clause in subjunctive contexts.
conditions: Action in dependent clause is anterior to main clause.
agreement_rules: Past participle agrees with subject when auxiliary is être.

attestations.source_text: The past subjunctive is used in the same way as the present subjunctive. In such sentences, the action of the dependent clause is anterior to the action of the main clause. To form the past subjunctive, use the present subjunctive of avoir or être + the past participle of the verb.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Penser/croire: affirmative vs negative/interrogative
exceptions_and_traps.description: Affirmative penser/croire is followed by the indicative; negative/interrogative may use the subjunctive to express doubt.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: Je ne crois pas que Daniel soit coupable. (subjunctive, doubt)
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: Je crois que Daniel soit coupable. (incorrect use of subjunctive after affirmative)

attestations.source_text: The verbs penser (to think) and croire (to believe) in the affirmative are followed by the indicative mood. However, in the negative and interrogative, the subjunctive can be used to underline the uncertainty of the event.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Impersonal expressions: indicative vs subjunctive
exceptions_and_traps.description: Some impersonal expressions take the indicative, others take the subjunctive. The lists must be memorized.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: Il est certain qu'il viendra. (indicative) / Il est possible qu'il vienne. (subjunctive)
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: Il est certain qu'il vienne. (incorrect use of subjunctive after certainty expression)

attestations.source_text: Let's compare the use of the indicative and the subjunctive with some impersonal expressions: Il est certain qu'il viendra ce soir. / Il est possible qu'il vienne ce soir.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Pourvu que: 'provided that' vs hope
exceptions_and_traps.description: Pourvu que can mean 'provided that' in a two-clause structure, or express hope in a single clause.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: Il ne démissionnera pas pourvu que le directeur lui donne une augmentation. (provided that) / Pourvu qu'il y ait un cybercafé! (hope)
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: Using 'provided that' in a single-clause exclamation or vice versa.

attestations.source_text: Pourvu que has the sense of provided that. ... When used in a single clause, pourvu que takes a different meaning. It is a handy expression, also followed by the subjunctive, that expresses hopes and desires.
